opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most important things we've learned over the last couple of years. When we started, there was this idea that you'd just train the biggest general model you can, put it behind an API, and every company would plug into it and be done. And in practice, that's not really how it works for a lot of enterprises.

What we see is that the off-the-shelf model gets you maybe 70 or 80 percent of the way there on a given use case, but the last 20 percent is where all the value is for the customer. And that last part usually depends on their own data, their internal terminology, their workflows, sometimes very specific formats or languages or regulatory constraints. A general model has never seen any of that, so it can't magically be good at it.

So the way we think about it is, first, you want strong base models, ideally ones that are efficient enough that customers can actually deploy them wherever they need, on their own infrastructure, on-prem, in their own cloud, because a lot of these companies simply can't send their data to an external API. Then on top of that, you work with them to adapt the model: fine-tuning on their data, sometimes continued pretraining if the domain is really different, building good evaluation sets that reflect what they actually care about, and setting up the whole pipeline around it, retrieval, tool use, agents and so on.

And honestly, the evaluation part is often underestimated. Many companies don't really know how to measure whether a model is good for their task. So a big part of the work is helping them define that, because once you have a good eval, you can iterate very quickly and you can show that a smaller, customized model actually beats a much larger generic one on their problem, and it's cheaper and faster to serve.

Also, it's a very nice feedback loop for us as a research team. Working closely with customers tells us where the models are failing in the real world, which is often quite different from what the public benchmarks measure. That feeds back into how we train the next generation of models. So for us, it's not really a choice between doing research and serving enterprises. The two kind of reinforce each other.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that when we started Mistral, the bet was that open weights would matter a lot for enterprises, and that's turned out to be true for reasons that are maybe a bit different from what people expected. It's not just about cost, it's about control. A lot of the companies we talk to, especially in Europe, in finance, in defense, in healthcare, they simply cannot send their data to an API somewhere. They need the model to run in their own environment, on their own infrastructure, sometimes fully air-gapped. So the starting point is: can you actually deploy this thing where the data lives? If the answer is no, the conversation is over before it starts.

The second thing is that "tailored" doesn't usually mean what people think. Most enterprises don't need a model trained from scratch on their data. That's very expensive and honestly not that useful. What they need is a strong base model that they can adapt, and the adaptation can be quite light. Fine-tuning on a few thousand examples, sometimes just good retrieval on top of their documents, sometimes a small model that's been distilled for one very specific task so it's cheap enough to run on every transaction. The art is in figuring out which of those you actually need, and that requires sitting with the customer and understanding the workflow, not just the data.

And then there's the question of how much you do yourself versus how much you give them the tools to do. Our view has been that we should be able to do both. Some customers have strong ML teams and they just want the weights and the fine-tuning recipes and they'll take it from there. Others have no ML team at all, and for them we'll go much deeper, we'll build the pipeline, we'll help with evaluation, we'll deploy. Evaluation is actually where most of the time goes, by the way. Everyone underestimates it. You can fine-tune a model in an afternoon, but knowing whether it's actually better for their use case, that takes weeks of work building the right test sets with their domain experts.

I think the mistake a lot of labs make is treating enterprise as a distribution channel for a frontier model. Like, here's the API, go build something. That works for startups. It doesn't work for a bank. For them the model is maybe twenty percent of the problem, and the other eighty percent is latency, compliance, integrating with systems from 2005, making sure the thing doesn't hallucinate on a contract clause. So we try to build the model with those constraints in mind from the beginning, which is partly why we care so much about efficiency, small models, mixture of experts. A model that's slightly less capable but that you can actually run on the hardware you have is worth much more to these customers than one that's a few points better on a benchmark but can only live in someone else's data center.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is understanding what the customer is actually trying to accomplish. “We want to use AI” is not quite a use case. You need to identify a specific workflow, understand what a good result looks like, and decide how you’re going to measure whether the system is useful.

Then you can work backward to the technical solution. Does the model need access to internal documents? Does it need to interact with existing software? Are there constraints around latency, cost, or where the data can be processed? Those questions should drive the architecture, including whether you need to fine-tune a model at all.

The balance is between adapting to the customer and building something repeatable. You want to solve their particular problem, but ideally the underlying capabilities can support many customers. And you need a feedback loop with the people actually using it, because a convincing demo and a system that works reliably in their daily workflow are very different milestones.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to understand what the customer is actually trying to do. “We want to use AI” is not a very precise problem. You want to identify a workflow where you can measure whether the system is useful, and then understand the constraints: what data it needs, where it can run, the latency, the cost.

Then you can decide what needs to be tailored. Sometimes it’s giving the model access to the right information and tools. Sometimes you need fine-tuning for a particular task. You don’t necessarily need a different model for every customer.

The important thing is to have a feedback loop with the people using it. You start with something concrete, evaluate it on real examples, understand where it fails, and improve it. A model that looks impressive in a demo is only one part of building something that works reliably in a business.
